extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military lawyers, and military officers interpreting and applying the Articles of War
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying legal standards, definitions, jurisdictional rules, and interpretive criteria for offenses and procedures under the Articles of War (court-martial practice and related military law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to act as an officer's servant not violation of 21st article
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the refusal of a soldier to comply with an order to act as an officer's servant is not a violation of the twenty-first article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions: R. 11, 80, July 21, 1880; C. 22404, Nov. 25, 1907. See also R.S. sec. 1232 forbidding use of enlisted man as a servant; but findings disapproving convictions where such orders were unlawful (G.C.M.O. 130, Dept. of Dakota, 1879).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to contract marriage when ordered not violation of 21st article
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the refusal of a soldier to contract marriage when ordered to do so was not a violation of the twenty-first article of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal by post band to play for civilians not violation of 21st article
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the refusal by a member of a post band to obey an order of a post commander to play in a neighboring town for the pleasure of the inhabitants was not a violation of the twenty-first article of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal of prophylactic treatment treated differently from disobedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where a soldier refuses prophylactic medical treatment on religious or personal-health grounds are peculiar and affect the person; punishment for such refusal is regarded differently than punishment for violation of orders directly pertaining to military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested approval of purchase of discharge in lieu of forcing treatment; cited correspondence C.11753 Jan. 26, 1912 and Feb. 9, 1912 — recommended discharge without honor under changed conditions after trial and sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to obey orders of doubtful legality (XXI D)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier receives an order of doubtful legality, it is his duty to obey and seek redress afterwards; disobedience in the first instance is an offense under the sixty-second article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: illiterate soldier ordered to copy his name refused — refusal was an offense under article 62. Cited: P.27, 444, Nov. 1888; C.9709, June 26, 1901.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and charges for killing a superior officer (XXI E 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier kills his superior officer on a military reservation ceded to the United States, he may be tried for murder in Federal court or for manslaughter under article 62, and for shooting his superior officer in violation of the twenty-first article of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital punishment may be imposed for aggravated peacetime violations (XXI E 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital sentences imposed and executed in time of war for violation of the twenty-first article do not deprive a court-martial of power to impose adequate punishment in peace-time when an offense is sufficiently aggravated to warrant capital punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: willful killing of a superior officer by an NCO was sufficiently aggravated to warrant capital sentence; cited C.21568, May 1, 1907.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mutiny (XXII A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutiny is unlawful opposing or resisting lawful military authority with intent to subvert it or nullify it for the time; intent distinguishes mutiny from other offenses including those under article 21 or 'mutinous conduct' under article 62.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutiny offenses are not necessarily aggregate or joint; beginning or causing mutiny may be committed by a single person but generally is concerted. Charging a mere act of insubordination as capital mutiny absent intent is improper; such acts should be charged under articles 20, 21, or 62. Citations: P.26,284 Sept. 1887; R.29,571 Jan. 1870; 38,199 July 1876.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal in combination to obey an unlawful order is not mutiny (XXII B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soldiers cannot properly be charged with joining in a mutiny where their act consists of refusing, in combination, to comply with an unlawful order — e.g., volunteers enlisted for a particular service who refuse to be used for different service are not chargeable with mutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating such refusal as capital was technical and unjust. Cited: R.42,524 Mar. 1880.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 25 authorizes preventive measures, not punishment (XXV A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 25 confers no jurisdiction or power to punish on courts-martial but authorizes taking certain measures of prevention and restraint by commanding officers to prevent serious disorders (e.g., duels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a challenge to duel (XXVI A)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that a challenge was sent, there must have been communicated a deliberate invitation in terms or substance to engage in personal combat with deadly weapons to obtain satisfaction for wounded honor; mere willingness to fight or language of hostility is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous language may still amount to a challenge if the intention is reasonably implied; surrounding circumstances and prior communications may be admissible to show intent. Cites to dueling code and many General Orders: R.39,247 Oct. 1877 and cited cases and orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29th article limited to wrongs by regimental commanders (XXIX A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The twenty-ninth article is expressly limited to wrongs alleged to have been committed by regimental commanders and does not apply to other commanding officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions: R.55,365 Mar. 22, 1888; C.18317, July 19, 1905; 18387, Aug. 4, 1905; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malice required to show 'wronged' under 29th article (XXIX B)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a regimental commander reports facts on an officer's efficiency report, the officer is not 'wronged' under the 29th article unless it is clearly shown that the report was malicious and not dictated by a true sense of duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regimental court under article 30 not a trial of officers (XXX A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 30 does not contemplate trial of an officer but an investigation and adjustment of matters in dispute (accountability, right to pay, allowance, relief from stoppage); the regimental court acts as a board and should reach a definite opinion sufficiently specific for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: R.23,631 July 1867; 28,113 Aug. 1868; others. Regimental court has no power to find 'guilty' or 'not guilty' or to sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings under article 30 are not affected by article 103 limits (XXX B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceeding under article 30, not being a trial, is not affected by the limitation of the 103rd article; nevertheless due diligence should be exercised in presenting complaints and undue delay (e.g., three years unexcused) may prejudice the complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only regimental commander can summon regimental court (XXX C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to summon a regimental court under article 30 is vested in terms in the regimental commander; a department or superior commander cannot properly exercise such authority nor make the proceeding valid by his order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to jurisdiction of regimental court (XXX D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two unqualified limitations: (1) it cannot usurp the place of a court of inquiry; (2) it can take no cognizance of matters beyond the power of the regimental commander to redress — matters requiring punishment of an officer are beyond its province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If matter is beyond the commander's reach it is beyond the court's jurisdiction; examples: wrongs requiring punishment of officer. Cases: P.43,37,479 Sept./Nov. 1890; C.855 Jan. 1895.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to complain under article 38 not prejudiced by regulations (XXX E)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to complain vested in enlisted men by the thirty-eighth article is a statutory right and its exercise cannot be prejudiced by requirements of regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence from quarters vs absence from troop/command (XXXII A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An unauthorized absence from the quarters only (e.g., from 11 p.m. inspection) is not properly chargeable under the thirty-second article; article 32 contemplates absence from the soldier's troop, battery, company, or detachment — i.e., absence from post or command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations of article 33 should not be charged under article 32
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the thirty-third article only should not be charged as absence without leave under the thirty-second article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent charges under articles 32 and 33 possible (XXXII B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier absent without leave who fails to repair to place of parade, etc., may be charged under both the thirty-second and thirty-third articles of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence to evade practice march may trigger multiple charges (XXXII C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier absents himself without leave for a definite period with apparent purpose of evading an announced practice march, he may be charged with a violation of article 32 and also of article 62 for attempt to evade the practice march.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness offense not limited to alcohol (XXXVIII A)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is immaterial whether drunkenness is voluntarily induced by spirituous liquor or by opium or other intoxicating drug; in either case the offense may be equally complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post commander deemed always on duty for drunkenness charge (XXXVIII B1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A post commander, while present and exercising command, is deemed to be at all times on duty in the sense of this article, and thus liable to a charge under it if found drunk at post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical officer may be 'on duty' all day for drunkenness (XXXVIII B2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A medical officer of a post with constantly sick persons under his charge may generally be deemed 'on duty' during the whole day and may be charged if found drunk at any hour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer reporting while drunk is chargeable (XXXVIII B3)
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer reporting in person drunk upon arrival at a post to which he was ordered to report is chargeable; similarly reporting drunk to post commander for orders as officer of the day after being detailed as such is chargeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not 'drunk on duty' unless permitted to enter duty (XXXVIII B3a)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer or soldier is found drunk at the time he is required to enter upon a duty, he is not 'drunk on duty' unless he shall be permitted to enter the duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found drunk on duty is sufficient regardless of when drunkenness commenced (XXXVIII C1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier found drunk when on duty may be convicted though his drunkenness commenced before going on duty; offense is being 'found drunk' on duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.31,334 Apr. 1871; C.15376 Oct. 13, 1903; C.25940 Jan. 15, 1910. It is also an offense to knowingly allow a soldier under influence to go on duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentinel 'on post' defined broadly (XXXIX A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentinel is on post within the meaning of the thirty-ninth article when walking a duly designated sentinel's post (ordinary garrison), or when stationed in observation against approach of enemy, to maintain internal discipline, guard stores, or guard prisoners in confinement or at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized absence from guard place triable under article 40 (XL A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any unauthorized absence from the place of a guard by a member of the guard may properly be tried under the fortieth article of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misbehavior before the enemy defined (XLII A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misbehavior before the enemy may be cowardice, willful violation of orders, gross negligence or inefficiency, act of treason or treachery, etc.; need not be in actual sight of the enemy but enemy must be in the neighborhood and the act must relate to operations directed against or growing out of the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be committed in Indian, foreign or civil war. Cites: R.6,79 Apr. 1864; P. 174 Dec. 1864; others. Examples and General Orders cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'his arms or ammunition' (XLII B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'his arms or ammunition' does not refer to arms personally owned by a soldier but means such as have been furnished to him by the proper officer for use in the service; construed with 'his post or colors.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilians amenable to court-martial in certain circumstances (XLV A)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the War of the Rebellion civilians, equally with military persons, were held amenable to trial and punishment by court-martial under articles treating certain offenses when acts were committed on theater of war or under martial law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions: R.2,498 June 1863; 5,291 Nov. 1863; 11,215,454 Dec. 1864/Feb. 1865. Note limitations where not under military government (Ex parte Milligan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inhabitants of insurgent states prima facie enemies (XLV B)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the War of the Rebellion all inhabitants of insurrectionary States were prima facie enemies in the sense of this and succeeding articles; a citizen of an insurgent State who entered U.S. military service ceased to be an enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relieving the enemy includes exchanges for valuable commodities (XLV C)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no less a relieving of the enemy that money etc. furnished is exchanged for some commodity (e.g., cotton) valuable to the other party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.12,386 Mar. 1865; R.14,266 Mar. 1865; contrasting relief with trading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief distinguished from trading with the enemy (XLV C1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of 'relieving the enemy' contemplated by the article is restricted to certain specific forms of relief, while trading with the enemy (a separate offense) includes every kind of commercial intercourse not expressly authorized by the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.14,266 Mar. 1865. See War section for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence with the enemy completed by writing and putting letter in progress (XLVI A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The offense of holding correspondence with the enemy is completed by writing and putting in progress a letter to an inhabitant of an insurrectionary State; it is not essential that the letter reach its destination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving intelligence requires actual communication of material information (XLVI B)
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute the offense of giving intelligence to the enemy, material information must actually be communicated to him; the communication may be verbal, written, or by signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning deserter to duty without trial implies admission of desertion (XLVIII A)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a deserter is returned to duty without trial there is an implied admission on his part of the desertion; this admission establishes the desertion and triggers the requirement that he make good the time lost in desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States may waive liability to make good time by discharging deserter (XLVIII B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States may waive the liability imposed by the first clause of the article; waiver occurs where the deserter is discharged by an official authorized by article 4 or adjudged dishonorably discharged by sentence duly approved and executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making good time becomes operative after court-martial conviction (XLVIII C1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a conviction by court-martial for desertion, where the sentence does not include discharge, the requirement to make good time lost becomes operative by its own force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability to make good time independent of punishment adjudged (XLVIII C2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability to make good to the United States the time lost by desertion is independent of any punishment which may be imposed by court-martial; it need not be adjudged or mentioned in terms in a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.50,413 June 1886. If sentence disapproved legal status is as if acquitted and obligation of additional service not incurred (R.26,668 June 1868).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of making-good-time postponed until after execution of punishment (XLVIII C3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of the liability is postponed until after execution of punishment (if any); a deserter may still be required to make good time even though his term of enlistment has expired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disapproval of conviction wipes out liability to make good time (XLVIII C4 / XLVIII D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disapproval of a conviction operates as an acquittal; a soldier whose conviction of desertion has been disapproved cannot be required to make good time lost. Making-good-time provision considered penal; if acquitted liability is wiped out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making-good-time requires actual military service; excludes time awaiting trial or serving sentence (XLVIII E)
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that a deserter serve such period as, with time previously served, will amount to full enlistment requires military service and excludes time spent while awaiting trial or serving sentence; deserter does not begin to serve unexpired portion until completing sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.30,606 July 15, 1870; R.31,275,374 Mar./May 1871; multiple citations C. 16306 et al.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability to trial/punishment subject to statute of limitations but making-good-time continues (XLVIII F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability to trial and punishment under the second clause of the article is subject to the limitation of prosecutions prescribed in article 103; however, liability to make good time lost continues even though statute of limitations has run as to prosecution.
